title: Vasquez: fear can accompany determinate opinion; doubt is hesitation between both sides
source_text: IX. Sic formidinem & dubitationem distinguit & explicat Vasquez: Omnis, inquit, formido sine dubitatione oppositae partis esse potest. Dubitatio enim est haesitatio intellectus inter utramque partem contradictionis, ita ut in neutra parte ei appareat convenientia extremorum inter se, in cujus cognitione assensus consistit. Formido autem non oritur ex dubio inter utramque partem contradictionis, si quidem esse potest cum determinato assensu opinionis: sed oritur ex judicio quodam reflexo, quo quis expendens principia, ex quibus deduxit assensum, judicat ea talis esse naturae, ut fortassis illud de quo est opinio in re aliter sit quam apparet: quod judicium esse potest extrinseca principia, & ita cum assensu determinato alterius partis reperiri supra monuimus. In primam secundae, Tom. 1. Disp. 200. cap. 8. sub finem.
pass_a_gloss: Thus Vasquez distinguishes and explains fear and doubt: Every fear, he says, can exist without doubt of the opposite side. For doubt is a hesitation of the intellect between both sides of the contradiction, so that on neither side does the fitting of the extremes to each other appear to it, in knowledge of which assent consists. But fear does not arise from doubt between both sides of the contradiction, since indeed it can exist with the determinate assent of opinion; but it arises from a certain reflex judgment by which someone, weighing the principles from which he deduced assent, judges them to be of such a nature that perhaps that about which there is opinion is in the thing otherwise than it appears—which judgment can be from extrinsic principles, and so, as we warned above, can be found together with determinate assent to the other side. On the First of the Second, volume 1, Disputation 200, chapter 8, toward the end.
pass_b_english: Vasquez defines doubt as intellective hesitation between contradictories.
Fear is a reflex judgment that principles might fail—compatible with firm opinionated assent.
